content:
When I do pen-and-paper math in my workbooks, I follow a fairly linear path in my logic. I will start with the core truths of the problem, and then derive structural truth through algebraic manipulation of the forms based on the constraints of the problem and basically keep following that kind of pattern until I realize an end result. As a self-taught programmer, I often follow the same kind of architectural logic where I will have a direct pipeline of functions calling each-other in a chain from the core layer all the way out to the end. It works.

I have a natural inclination to do the same thing in Lean, but the AI (multiple models) warns me against it.

The lesson the AI wants me to learn, is that lean (and formal theorem proving) wants me to define objects within layers, and prove equivalencies between these things, and then work with the "higher order" definitions as I move to downstream layers, rather than directly daisy-chaining a long line of lemmas through multiple layers. So there are these kind of definitional stepping stones in each layer, bridged by equivalence lemmas. I can see that there is an equivalence to my own work, but the abstraction still bothers me...

Is the AI correct?

The right definitions can make your life much easier, this is true in both programming and proving. For example, parser combinators are nicer that a hand-written recursive descent, array programming is nicer than explicit for loops, and so on.

Nothing stops you from unfolding definitions, but the result is usually ugly.

You don't necessary need "equivalence lemmas", all you need are just the right definitions and the right lemmas. What's "right" is also a matter of taste, so AI is of no help here.

Well, my issue is that the problem i am working on is highly contentious (or at least, anything claiming to be a proof is), so the motivation for me is to avoid as many definitional inclusions as possible. If everything is derived from primitives and first principles, and it typechecks, then there is a lot less room for error or arguments, like "is that truly the right definition" or even worse "did you accidentally introduce a circular tautology here?" That's how I developed my theory in my notebooks, but implementing it in lean is not so straight forward for me.
I'm not sure I quite follow your question, but I suspect you'll learn most from just trying your approach

I would say the AI has a point. Imagine trying to do pencil and paper mathematics except that you are restricted to using the core steps in geometry (you aren't allowed subroutines) or in the language used by Russell and Whitehead in P.M. Even if you are conversant in either language, I don't see you doing this purely in that language without a mental model of the outline or overview: you have a "map" of the territory which has none of the core steps but has evidence that sequences of core steps can get you from one point on the map to another. I could make a similar remark about writing in assembly or C.

You could approach programming in Lean as trying to take various statements, drill down for each statement to the core version using only primitives, and then trying to find at this same core level paths of manipulations of proof terms to get from one statement to the other. Or, you could try seeing the various statements as an architectural blueprint which helps you see the relations between the various pieces in high level terms, and slowly refine and develop the statements and relations in more and more detail until you reach the core level. This second way allows you to anticipate what steps and patterns of steps are reusable, and then develop machinery that "allows you to take bigger steps on the map". Along with Ruben, you will appreciate this perspective and the AI's point only after fighting with (or working with) it for a while.
sender_full_name: J. J. Issai (project started by GRP)

My approach to the map is global, also in my workbooks. But I built up a sequential chain of logic to get there. I guess I am just overly cautious or overly zealous in having as rigorous a description in lean as possible. Doubly so as I am not yet fluent in lean (learning!), so having something sneak in would be most unfortunate.

I appreciate the insights.
